description: Somos un equipo interesado en la tecnología, la salud y la exploración espacial. Queremos crear una solución que ayude a los astronautas a cuidar su bienestar durante misiones largas. Buscamos personas creativas y comprometidas, con conocimientos de programación, diseño, salud o análisis de datos, y con ganas de aportar y aprender en equipo.
summary:
LifeNix is an intelligent health monitoring system designed to support the safety and autonomy of astronauts during space missions.

Our prototype uses sensors connected to an ESP32 to measure heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, and movement. The data is transmitted through a local network to a web platform that works without the internet.

Our main innovation is combining Machine Learning (Isolation Forest) with a custom mathematical model, allowing us to analyze physiological patterns, identify deviations from normal values, and generate smart alerts.

LifeNix is a modular and scalable platform, with the potential to incorporate new sensors and monitor entire crews. As a next step, we propose developing smart gloves with integrated sensors to make monitoring easier.

We aim to complement current spatial monitoring systems, making it easier to interpret vital signs and detect abnormalities. Also, this technology could be adapted for remote communities on Earth, where connectivity and access to medical services are limited. 

LifeNix turns physiological data into useful information to help make timely decisions.
details:
LIFENIX – Offline Health Monitoring for Astronauts

What does it do and how does it work?
LIFENIX is a visual health-monitoring tool that helps astronauts check their own health on board, without internet. Wearable sensors measure heart rate and blood oxygen (MAX30102), skin temperature (MLX90614) and body movement (MPU6050). A microcontroller sends one reading per second over a local Wi-Fi network to a laptop. There, a FastAPI backend stores the data in SQLite and analyzes it in three layers: fixed physiological rules (traffic-light thresholds), a machine-learning model (Isolation Forest) and a personal statistical baseline (z-scores combined into a distance evaluated with a chi-square distribution). The web dashboard shows live vital signs, charts over time, a color-coded status (green, yellow, red, grey), a 3D astronaut whose head, lungs and heart are clickable, an AI risk index from 0 to 100, and general, prudent recommendations for action. Astronauts can also log their daily sleep hours and mood.

Benefits

  • Works fully offline, as a real long-duration mission requires, where help from Earth is delayed or cut off.
  • Reduces false alarms: the model takes physical activity into account, so normal exercise does not trigger a red alert.
  • Explainable safety: red alerts are always decided by physiological rules. The AI can only add caution (yellow) or lower a false alarm caused by exercise.
  • Easy to understand: colors, simple explanations and a FAQ assistant (“Silvia”) that answers questions with live data and an optional voice.

Expected impact
LIFENIX supports astronauts’ autonomy in health self-assessment and addresses NASA Human Research Program hazards: distance from Earth, altered gravity (cardiovascular changes), hostile closed environments (oxygen and temperature) and isolation (sleep and mood). It is a decision-support tool, not a medical diagnosis.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Hardware: ESP32, MAX30102, GY-906 MLX90614, GY-521 MPU6050 (I2C bus).
  • Firmware: C++ in Arduino IDE.
  • Backend: Python 3.13, FastAPI, Uvicorn, SQLite.
  • AI and statistics: scikit-learn (Isolation Forest), personal baseline model (z-scores + chi-square).
  • Dashboard: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Chart.js and Google model-viewer with a NASA 3D Resources astronaut model, all stored locally.
  • Tools: VS Code, GitHub. All free and open-source.

How is it creative?
It combines real sensors, machine learning and an explainable statistical model in a hybrid system, where the AI understands context (rest vs. exercise) and each person’s normal values. The interactive 3D astronaut turns data into something visual and intuitive. A built-in simulation mode keeps the tool working even if a sensor fails.

What did the team consider?

  • Safety first: conservative recommendations, with red alerts always decided by rules.
  • A backup plan for every layer: simulated data if the hardware fails, rules only if the model fails, a phone hotspot if the Wi-Fi fails.
  • Real sensor limitations: skin temperature instead of core temperature, and no pulse reading during movement.
  • Training the model with real sensor data recorded by the team.
  • Prior development: authorized in advance by our local event organizers (Ica). Third-party libraries used: SparkFun MAX3010x, Adafruit MLX90614, scikit-learn, FastAPI, Chart.js and Google model-viewer.
